title: Learning Go, and someone else's codebase, under pressure
question: Tell me about a time you were pushed outside your comfort zone

situation: The existing Java code that optimised AWS Lambda function ZIP packages, with and without layers, and transformed them into the data plane format, ran in some cases synchronously and had no concept of state, something we needed to introduce to move the code to an asynchronous model. The async path relied on S3 notifications, which wasn't optimal: it triggered Lambda functions multiple times and required workarounds to skip the redundant invocations. I hadn't been part of the initiative from the start, and Go, the language chosen for the rewrite, was new to me.
task: I was put in charge of designing and implementing a high-performance replacement service in Go supporting both SQS-driven and direct HTTP invocation, and of refactoring the control plane orchestration so it handled function layer edge cases cleanly, all while ramping up on a language and a codebase that weren't mine to begin with.
action: Pipeline engineering in Go: I designed a concurrent, channel-based pipeline with adaptive interfaces for dual SQS and HTTP handling, replacing the legacy Java version and cutting processing latency by 50%.

Control plane refactoring: the Go pipeline work was well received, and on the strength of it I was asked to join an away team to refactor the orchestration service that fetches layers and organises storage. I ended up rewriting most of the component, with layers support as the biggest piece I added, alongside other edge cases, and built a rapid integration testing framework around it.
result: End-to-end package processing time halved, and automated test coverage held across the edge cases.

challenge: Safely executing the multi-phase migration from the legacy path to the new flow while the old code was still running, rolling out over days.
hardestBug: The team had decided to reuse the image function polling mechanism to handle copying function artifacts for new versions, without realising it wouldn't scale to the new load. In our biggest region, this caused failures that impacted not just ZIP functions but image functions as well, threatening control plane operations and blocking global rollouts. I designed a deduplication concept, along with all the required updates to the background jobs to handle it, within a week, eliminating the redundant function copies and getting rollouts moving again safely.
differently: I would push for end-to-end stress and performance testing under synthetic noisy-neighbour conditions early in the design phase. Our functional integration testing was exhaustive, but validating control plane behaviour under heavy concurrent load would have exposed the regional background job scaling limits before production did.
aboutYourself: I learned to be patient when diving into massive, unfamiliar codebases. Systems that feel overwhelming at first become manageable once you methodically trace the data flows, ask targeted questions, and build safety nets through testing frameworks.
enjoyed: Working directly with principal engineers in the US, debating complex distributed workflows and resolving high-impact system bottlenecks together.
